In flight: runs at 3,964 PF on a 16x pool, and input document subsampling combined with the token drop.
setup: Each method trains with its own forward, optimiser and real LR schedule on the same first batches of the pool (16 rows/step, 2 GPUs).

At fixed steps the dense forward (full context, no dropping, adapters on) is scored on held-out rows from the CTC-suite eval files: teacher-forced answer CE, 16 rows per task and length (4k, 8k, 16k) except reorder at 16k, where only 8 eval rows fit in 16,384 tokens; eval_size 184.

Score = training FLOPs the dense reference needs to reach a loss level divided by the FLOPs the method needs to reach the same level, on the mean loss and on the worst task. Peak GPU memory is logged per step.
One iteration is under 15 minutes. Every 2-3 hours the most promising methods get a larger FLOP-matched training run with generation-graded evals.

Data caveats: the 16k training cells use fewer documents per row than the eval (contradiction 324 vs 379, outlier 96 vs 111, reorder 90 vs 116) so rows fit in 16,384 tokens; the 16k held-out rows are the short tail of the eval rung (70, 303, 8 and 497 of 500 rows fit for contradiction, outlier, reorder, qdmatch_nq). About 46% of the documents in a qdmatch_nq held-out row also occur in training rows (no gold overlap, no prompt overlap).

For runs that stop before reaching a reference level, the table also gives iso-loss ratios at the run's own final loss: FLOPs the dense-LoRA reference (and the recipe) need to reach that loss divided by the run's FLOPs. These are generous to a run whose final loss is shallow, because the reference curves are only probed every 10-25 steps.

ideas.title: Current recipe (router, keep 20% after block 7, 7% after block 16)
ideas.what: The 8k recipe unchanged at 4k-16k on the new tasks, plus random keep at the same budget.
ideas.result: Recipe: 0.22x dense per step, 1.7x fewer FLOPs than the tuned dense-LoRA reference to the 100-step level, 1.4x on the worst task. Random keep at the same budget: 0.54x of the recipe's efficiency; random keep 9%: 0.42x; keep 10%/3.5%: 0.71x; 5%/2%: 0.55x; 2%/1%: 0.27x.

ideas.title: Frozen no-grad prefix + earlier cuts
ideas.what: Blocks 0-k run forward-only (no backward, no stored activations), tokens dropped from block 2-4 onward in more stages. Attacks the 0.2x/step floor of blocks 0-6 and the memory peak.
ideas.result: Negative. Freezing blocks 0-6 (forward-only) with the recipe's cuts: 0.149x dense per step, 0.282 held-out CE at step 60 vs about 0.19 for the recipe; deeper freezing is worse (0.399 / 0.491 / 0.647 with the boundary at block 7 / 16 / 20 plus earlier cuts). Earlier cuts alone (first cut at block 2) also trail the recipe per FLOP. Transient memory is unchanged under activation checkpointing. The gradient into the early blocks carries most of the learning. Branch loop/prefix.

ideas.title: Gold-aware stochastic keep
ideas.what: Per-document keep probability raised for gold documents but never 1 and never 0 for distractors, so the kept set does not reveal the answer; drop before block 0 as well as mid-stack.
ideas.result: Mixed. Best arm grJ (0.133x dense per step): 1.26x the recipe at matched loss on the main pool at step 108, but on the 50/50 pool gold-aware arms are level with or behind the plain recipe on that pool, so the two gains do not stack. The cheapest arms (0.07-0.08x) stay shallow (0.27-0.34 held-out CE). Per task (46 rows each): grJ is worse than the plain recipe on outlier (0.169, flat from step 25, against 0.10-0.13) and ahead on contradiction; the gain on the mean comes from the other three tasks.

ideas.title: Loss and backward through the first few blocks only
ideas.what: An early-exit answer loss after block k gives true per-token gradients at full length for the cost of k blocks; use them to pick tokens and to train the early blocks.
ideas.result: Negative. Selecting tokens by the gradient of an early-exit answer loss is worse than the ridge router at the recipe's keep (0.213 vs 0.175 held-out CE at step 75) and at 10%/3% (0.237 vs 0.224); it only wins at a very aggressive cut after block 2 (0.584 vs 0.763 at step 40), far from any reference level. The auxiliary early loss slows training; training the early blocks by the early loss alone fails (0.503). The frozen head at block 7 gives an early-exit CE near uniform, so its gradient is weak. Branch loop/earlyloss.

ideas.title: Detached context / reused context states
ideas.what: Context tokens run forward-only (or reuse cached states), gradient only through query and answer tokens; then drop context tokens aggressively in that no-grad pass.
ideas.result: Negative for FLOPs. Context forward-only from block 0, no drops: 0.15x of the recipe's efficiency; from block 7: 0.354 at step 97; from block 16: 0.207 at 131 PF vs the recipe's 0.145; with a 1,024-token gradient tail: 0.375 at step 173; every 4th step dense: 0.44x of the recipe. The memory arms with activation checkpointing off produced no result. Branch loop/detach.

ideas.title: FLOP-aware row sampling and row skipping
ideas.what: Sample rows by expected loss decrease per FLOP (short rows more often, a tail of 16k rows), skip rows a cheap early-exit loss marks as solved.
ideas.result: Recipe on rows <= 5k: 3.2-3.4x vs dense LoRA down to held-out CE 0.125, then it plateaus at 0.119 (no 8k / 16k rows). Length curriculum on the 50/50 pool: 2.7-3.4x, no better than the static mix. Token-budget batches help dense LoRA (1.4-1.5x) more than the recipe.

ideas.title: Label-consistent sub-problems
ideas.what: Train on a random subset of a row's documents with the answer rewritten for the subset (reorder, qdmatch), mixed with a few full rows.
ideas.result: Works. Recipe on the 80/20 short/long pool: 3.1-3.4x fewer FLOPs than dense LoRA at held-out CE 0.125 (two seeds); 50/50 pool: 2.9-3.0x; plain recipe 1.9-2.2x. Short rows alone fall behind. Dense LoRA on the same pools gains less (1.4-1.5x with token-budget batches). Next: 90% and 95% short, long tail only at 16k, short part only at 1k, full-epoch runs. On the 16k rows alone the mixed pools are only about 1.1-1.2x ahead of the plain recipe (56 rows, noisy). Update 11-17 afternoon, 16k held-out set (320 rows): with 3x the rows (1,464 steps, two seeds) the 80/20 pool reaches 0.134-0.136 at 479 PF against 0.145-0.150 for the plain recipe at 442 PF; at equal FLOPs the two are about level, so the advantage at shallow levels does not hold at depth on 16k. Pools with 90% / 95% short rows, the long part all at 16k, or the short part all at 1k are behind the 80/20 pool.

ideas.title: Skip the FFN for context tokens
ideas.what: Context tokens stay in attention / GDN mixing but skip most FFNs, instead of leaving the sequence.
ideas.result: Negative. Body tokens skipping the FFN in blocks 0-6 with probability 0.5: 0.193x dense per step (the recipe is 0.220x) but 0.274 held-out CE at step 50 vs the recipe's 0.201. Skipping every body-token FFN in blocks 0-3 stops learning (0.779 at step 50): training adapts to FFN-free tokens and the dense eval forward runs every FFN. Ceiling of the idea: the FFN is 41-62% of a block's per-token FLOPs. Branch loop/ffnskip.

ideas.title: Start from a base with token-drop continued pre-training
ideas.what: Look for existing drop-CPT checkpoints and test whether aggressive dropping loses less from such a base. No CPT runs inside the loop.
ideas.result: Router recipe from the token-exit CPT base and the dense-CPT control: 0.65-0.77x of the recipe's efficiency at matched loss, no better than the standard base at the same keep (0.71x at keep 10%/3.5%). No benefit from the drop-CPT base in this proxy.

ideas.title: LR, batch size and schedule per FLOP
ideas.what: Cheap arms can afford more, smaller steps: rows per step, LR and warmup tuned per FLOP rather than per step.
ideas.result: Recipe at LR 2e-5: 0.85x; LR 4e-5: 0.61x; 8 rows/step: 0.74x; 8 rows/step at LR 2e-5: 0.62x of the recipe's efficiency at matched loss. Dense LoRA: LR 2e-5 slightly better than 1e-5 (0.126 vs 0.131 at step 100), LR 4e-5 worse (0.170). The 8 rows/step arms are fastest only to the shallowest loss level and never reach the deeper ones. Schedule shape (warmup, decay) was not varied.

ideas.title: Drop-CPT bases fine-tuned in their own token-exit format
ideas.what: Token exit at block 8 and at the input (first+last rule), from the matching CPT base and from the standard base, at fixed compression 0.2 / 0.1 / 0.05.
ideas.result: Negative. Input-level token exit (first+last rule, keep 5-10%) improves for 25-50 steps and then degrades on the dense probe from both the standard and the drop-CPT base (never below 0.69). Exit at block 8, keep 10%: 0.233 (CPT base) vs 0.238 (standard base) at step 93, a tie, both behind the recipe. The CPT bases start 0.25-0.32 held-out CE worse than the standard base on these tasks.

ideas.title: Multi-question rows
ideas.what: Each row keeps its original question and answer, then appends 8-32 short sub-questions derived from its gold (which passage follows X, which document matches query j, which claim contradicts claim i, is document i an outlier). The context is paid for once; the extra answers cost only their own tokens.
ideas.result: Negative. Recipe on multi-question rows: 0.124 held-out CE at 220 PF vs the plain recipe's 0.124 at 180-210 PF; on the 50/50 pool 0.124 at 161 PF vs 0.125 at 135 PF. The sub-answers add 2-3x the supervised tokens but dilute the main answer's loss; a weighted variant was not tried.

ideas.title: Loss-proportional task and length sampling
ideas.what: Sample the next rows by each task-and-length cell's running training loss per FLOP instead of uniformly (reorder holds 5x the loss of the other tasks); row-level backward skipping; per-row vs per-token loss averaging.
ideas.result: No gain at 16k. Loss-per-cost sampling of task and length cells is level with the plain recipe on the same pool on the 16k held-out rows (1.0x on the 80/20 pool with two seeds, 0.9-1.0x on the 50/50 pool); its all-lengths gain is 1.0-1.3x and does not stack on the 80/20 pool. A stronger cost term (0.22 PF per step) stops the 16k loss tracking (0.90x). A 16k-targeted rule is level with the recipe at matched FLOPs. Loss-only sampling and a static reorder-heavy mix are level; per-row loss averaging starves reorder. No task is starved by the loss-per-cost rules. Branch loop/alloc.

ideas.title: Length-scaling breakdown and document-local attention in the early blocks
ideas.what: Tabulate where the recipe's FLOPs go at 4k-128k rows (the full-length attention of the early blocks is quadratic in length), then make that attention document-local during training so the early blocks' cost grows linearly with length.
ideas.result: Negative as a method; the FLOP breakdown stands. Recipe cost vs dense: 0.227 / 0.217 / 0.189 / 0.168 at 4k / 16k / 64k / 128k (flop meter's formulas; 32 blocks, 8 full attention at blocks 3, 7, ..., 31). Document-local attention in training hurts learning per step: block 3 only is 0.01-0.02 held-out CE behind the recipe at every step (0.246 / 0.181 / 0.164 / 0.144 vs 0.229 / 0.172 / 0.140 / 0.124) for a 2.8% FLOP saving, so it is worse at matched FLOPs at 16k; local attention in blocks 3-15 or in all attention blocks stalls training. A causal-mask control of the same attention path trains normally and the masked attention matches a dense reference, so this is a real effect, not a bug: documents need cross-document attention in training. The floor is the linear per-token cost of blocks 0-6 (0.118x dense, 54% of the recipe's step at 16k). Branch loop/lenscale.

ideas.title: Memory that stays flat at 256k-1M tokens
ideas.what: Measure how peak training memory grows with row length (16k-256k) for dense LoRA and the recipe, then run the early blocks chunk by chunk (no-grad pass, later blocks on the kept tokens, second chunked pass with gradient) with a kept-token budget fixed in tokens, so the peak is one chunk plus the kept tokens instead of the whole row.
ideas.result: Works. Measured transient memory above baseline for one step (1 H200, micro-batch 1, activation checkpointing on, synthetic long rows): dense LoRA 0.37 GiB per 1k tokens (52 GiB at 128k, out of memory at 256k); recipe 0.24 (65 GiB at 256k); early blocks in 4k chunks 0.10 (57 GiB at 512k); plus a 4,096-token keep cap 0.074 (79 GiB at 1M); plus host offload of the early blocks' checkpoint inputs 0.040 (45 GiB at 1M, 86 GiB at 2M). Longest row that fits on 141 GB: dense LoRA 128k, recipe 256k, chunked 512k, capped 1M, offloaded 2M. Learning at 16k is unchanged: held-out CE at steps 50 / 100 / 150 / 200 is 0.202 / 0.161 / 0.146 / 0.123 with 4k chunks vs 0.216 / 0.156 / 0.142 / 0.121 for the recipe, same FLOPs (one seed, eval_size 184); the chunked forward is bit-exact and the gradient's cosine to the exact gradient is 0.993-0.996 (0.97-0.98 in blocks 0-6). Not yet tested: learning at 64k and beyond, where the cut cross-chunk gradient paths are a larger share, and the keep cap's effect on learning. Branch loop/memscale (merged into the loop branch; flags off by default).

ideas.title: Long-range positions on short rows
ideas.what: Short rows only show the attention blocks distances below 2k. Give them positions that span 16k (stretching), and thin long rows by dropping whole documents at the input while keeping the survivors' original positions, so cheap rows carry long-range structure and fewer full long rows are needed for the 16k loss.
ideas.result: Mixed (one seed, 16k reading from 320 rows). Position-preserving document subsampling of long rows works: keeping 25% of the non-gold documents (45% of the tokens) on the all-long pool needs 1.23-1.35x fewer FLOPs than the plain recipe for the same 16k loss (about 3.1x vs dense LoRA at LR 2e-5) and ties the 80/20 pool where their FLOPs overlap; keeping 50% gives 1.10-1.16x. Position stretching of short rows does not help: a tie or slightly worse on the 80/20 pool (0.92x), and short rows alone stay far behind at 16k even when stretched (16k loss 0.46-0.57). Not yet tried: subsampling the long rows inside the 80/20 pool. Branch loop/longpos.

ideas.title: Dense baseline family: full fine-tune, LoRA, fixed re-mix
ideas.what: Under the 11-18 rule LoRA and a fixed short/long row mix belong to the dense baseline. Full-epoch dense full fine-tune on the standard pool (488 steps, 1,982 PF) and on the 80/20 re-mix with 3x the rows (1,464 steps), with 16k held-out probes; dense LoRA full epoch already exists. Each drop arm is compared with the dense run that uses the same adapter and pool.
ideas.result: Dense full fine-tune, full epoch, two seeds (16k held-out CE on 320 rows): 0.114 and 0.119 at step 488 (1,982 PF); seed 0 curve 0.255 / 0.210 / 0.161 / 0.135 / 0.122 at steps 50 / 100 / 200 / 300 / 400. Dense LoRA ends at 0.121 at 0.76x the step cost (step-400 level of dense full fine-tune at 1.20x fewer FLOPs). Running: dense LoRA seed 1, the 80/20 re-mix reference, dense LoRA at equal FLOPs on 4x the rows (642 steps) and dense full fine-tune on 2x the rows (976 steps).

ideas.title: Drop ladder: from near-dense to the recipe
ideas.what: Find where token dropping stops tracking dense per step. Same router, full fine-tuning, full epoch: keep 50% after block 16 (gentlest), keep 50% after block 7, keep 50% then 20%, keep 20% then 7% (the recipe's budgets); and with LoRA: 50% then 20%, 50% after block 16. Read: 16k held-out loss at the same step as the dense run with the same adapter, out to step 488.
ideas.result: Constant budgets, 16k CE at step 488 (320 rows; dense full fine-tune 0.114 / 0.119 on two seeds, dense LoRA 0.121). With LoRA the loss stays within 0.002 of dense LoRA down to about 0.28x dense per step: three stages 50% / 20% / 7% at blocks 7 / 16 / 24 0.123 at 0.29x, 50% then 10% 0.123 at 0.28x, 50% then 20% 0.125 / 0.123 at 0.32x; these reach dense full fine-tune's step-350 level (0.129) at 2.7-3.1x fewer FLOPs but not its final loss in one epoch. Cheaper breaks: 35% then 12% 0.131 at 0.27x, 20% then 7% 0.145-0.150 at 0.22x, a first cut at block 3 (50% / 30% / 15%) 0.152 at 0.23x. With full fine-tuning: 50% after block 16 0.118 at 0.72x, 50% after block 7 0.121 at 0.60x, 50% then 20% 0.126 / 0.119 at 0.44x, 20% then 7% 0.138 / 0.135 at 0.30x. Three-stage 50% / 20% / 7% repeats on seed 1 (0.121 at 0.29x). Deeper or more stages are worse: 50% / 10% / 5% 0.132 at 0.27x, four stages 50% / 30% / 15% / 7% 0.129 at 0.27x.

ideas.title: Dense steps mixed into dropped training
ideas.what: The recipe trains on a truncated forward but is scored on the dense forward. Every 4th step dense, or the last 20% of the steps dense, with LoRA and with full fine-tuning; cost rises from 0.22-0.30x to about 0.4x dense per step.
ideas.result: Interim (seed 0, 16k CE at step 488, 320 rows). Dense steps help the recipe but cost more than a gentler constant drop: recipe + every 4th step dense 0.129 at 0.36x, recipe + last 20% dense 0.131 at 0.33x, against LoRA keep 50% then 20% with no dense steps 0.125 at 0.32x. Full fine-tune versions: 0.130 at 0.48x and 0.128 at 0.44x, no better than full fine-tune keep 50% then 20% (0.126 at 0.44x).

ideas.title: Keep ramp over training
ideas.what: One cut after block 7 whose keep share rises linearly from 20% to 90% over the epoch (full fine-tuning): cheap steps early, near-dense steps at the end where the loss is deepest.
ideas.result: Corrected verdict: raising the keep share over training is within noise of dense at one epoch but is not better per FLOP than a constant budget. One epoch on the standard pool (16k CE at step 488, 320 rows; dense full fine-tune 0.114 / 0.119): the single-cut ramp 20% to 90% (0.64x per step) gave 0.113, 0.119 and 0.120 on three runs (two seeds plus a same-seed rerun through the new schedule flag), so the first 0.113 was a lucky draw and the earlier '1.6x at the dense final loss' was within noise. Other shapes, full fine-tune: both cuts ramped 20%/7% to 90%/90% 0.120 at 0.61x; 20%/7% held for half the run then ramped 0.120 at 0.46x (best value); ramp ending at 60%/40% 0.122 at 0.44x; held for 70% 0.124 at 0.41x; 10% to 90% 0.119 at 0.60x; ramp + dense last 10% 0.115 at 0.65x; starting at 10%/3% 0.138 at 0.44x; first cut at block 3 0.132 at 0.59x. With LoRA: 20% to 90% 0.120 at 0.48x. Budget-matched on the 4x pool at 1,980 PF the single-cut ramp ends at 0.088 (1.6x fewer FLOPs than the dense frontier), behind constant LoRA 50% / 20% / 7% (0.072) and 50% / 20% (0.078). Schedules are not pursued further. Code: branch loop/keepsched, flag --st-otr-stage-sched (piecewise keep per stage over training progress).

ideas.title: Adaptive keep by predicted gradient mass
ideas.what: Per document, keep the fewest tokens whose predicted gradient mass covers 99% / 95% / 90% (one cut after block 7, full fine-tuning). The budget is set per row by the router instead of a fixed share; a target of 100% is dense, so the target is a single dial from dense downwards.
ideas.result: No useful dial (seed 0, 16k CE at step 488, 320 rows). Covering 99 / 95 / 90% of the predicted gradient mass keeps most tokens: step cost 0.97x / 0.88x / 0.79x dense, CE 0.118 / 0.122 / 0.117. A fixed keep of 50% after block 7 gets 0.121 at 0.60x, so the mass target saves less for the same loss; the predicted mass is spread over too many tokens for a coverage threshold to cut deeply.

ideas.title: Dense forward, sparse backward
ideas.what: Every token stays in the forward pass (identical to the dense forward used for scoring); gradients flow only through the tokens the router keeps (20% above block 7, 7% above block 16). Separates the two things the recipe changes at once: no gradient for dropped tokens, and a truncated context for kept tokens. Ideal cost about 0.4-0.5x dense per step.
ideas.result: Diagnostic result (seed 0, 16k CE on 320 rows, full fine-tune). With the exact dense forward and gradients only through the kept tokens (20% above block 7, 7% above block 16) the loss is 0.136 at step 488, against 0.138 when the dropped tokens also leave the forward pass and 0.114 for dense: the gap to dense at steps 300-488 is +0.019 to +0.023 either way. So the recipe's gap comes from dropped tokens getting no gradient, not from kept tokens seeing a truncated context; removing tokens from the forward pass costs almost nothing extra once their gradient is gone. Sparse backward costs 0.54x dense per step (0.59x with one cut at block 7: 0.128; 0.50x with the cut at the input: 0.137) against 0.30x for forward dropping, so it is not a method to pursue; it reaches only dense's step-250 to step-350 level at 1.2-1.4x. Consequence for the search: what matters is how many tokens carry gradient and when (which is why raising the keep share late in training works). Branch loop/sparsebwd, flag --st-otr-sparse-bwd.

ideas.title: Mixture-of-depths: dropped tokens skip blocks but stay in the pass
ideas.what: From block 8 on, 80% of the document tokens skip 3 of every 4 blocks (or every other block) and rejoin at the others, so no token leaves the forward pass and kept tokens see the full context at the refresh blocks. Full fine-tuning.
ideas.result: Worse than plain dropping (seed 0, 16k CE at step 488, 320 rows): skipping 3 of every 4 blocks 0.137 at 0.66x dense per step, skipping every other block 0.134 at 0.77x, against 0.121 at 0.60x for dropping 50% of the tokens after block 7. Dropped.

ideas.title: Equal FLOPs, more rows: do cheap arms reach the dense final loss?
ideas.what: Give each arm the FLOPs of one dense full fine-tune epoch (1,982 PF) on a pool with 4x the rows, with its LR schedule stretched over its own step count: LoRA keep 50% then 20% (1,525 steps), LoRA keep 50% after block 16 (905), the old recipe 20% then 7% (1,952, the whole pool), full fine-tune keep 50% then 20% (1,108), and dense LoRA as the equal-FLOP baseline (642). The test of the deepest-loss rule: at equal FLOPs, which arm ends lowest, and how many FLOPs does each need to reach the dense full fine-tune final loss.
ideas.result: At about 1,980 PF on the 4x pool (16k CE, 320 rows, one seed each): LoRA 50%/20%/7% 0.072 (1,683 steps), LoRA 50%/20% 0.078 (1,525), full fine-tune 50%/20% 0.082 (1,108), recipe 20%/7% 0.083 (whole pool, 1,762 PF), keep ramp 0.088 (762), LoRA 50% after block 16 0.088 (905). Dense at the same FLOPs: dense LoRA with more rows 0.101, dense full fine-tune one epoch 0.114 / 0.119; dense full fine-tune needs 3,960 PF (976 steps) to reach 0.081. So cheap dropped steps on more rows beat dense at equal FLOPs by a wide margin, worth about 2x in FLOPs; see the budget-matched idea for the ratios.

ideas.title: Gradient compensation at the cut
ideas.what: The diagnosis says the loss gap is the gradient that dropped tokens no longer carry. Rescale, in the backward pass only, the gradient flowing through the kept document tokens at each cut by 1 / kept share (or 1 / the predicted gradient mass they cover, or its square root), so the blocks below the cut see a less biased update. Forward pass and FLOPs unchanged.
ideas.result: Does not help (seed 0, 16k CE at step 488, 320 rows; branch loop/gradcomp). At 20% / 7% every mode is worse than no compensation (0.138): 1/keep 0.160, 1/covered mass 0.153, sqrt(1/keep) 0.151. At 50% / 20%, 1/keep ends at 0.121 against 0.126 / 0.119 without: no difference. Rescaling the kept tokens' gradient does not stand in for the gradient of the dropped ones.

ideas.title: Does it matter which tokens carry the gradient?
ideas.what: At keep 50% then 20% with full fine-tuning: half of the kept budget drawn at random, and a fully random keep, against the router's top-scored tokens. If a random choice does as well, coverage across steps matters more than selection.
ideas.result: Selection matters (seed 0, 16k CE at step 488, 320 rows; full fine-tune, keep 50% then 20%, 0.44x): random tokens 0.132, half of the budget random 0.123, router 0.126 / 0.119 on two seeds; dense 0.114 / 0.119. A random keep is about 0.01 worse and stays 0.02-0.03 behind for most of the run; mixing in random tokens neither helps nor hurts.

ideas.title: Budget-matched FLOPs-to-match (complete schedules)
ideas.what: Every arm, dense included, gets a fixed FLOP budget (495 or 991 PF) on the 4x pool with its own complete LR schedule; the ratio is the FLOPs the dense frontier (dense full fine-tune and dense LoRA at every budget) needs for the arm's final loss, divided by the arm's FLOPs. This is the headline measure: it gives cheaper arms proportionally more steps and compares finished runs only.
ideas.result: Finished runs with complete schedules (16k CE on 320 rows, one seed each; seed-1 repeats of the headline points are running). Dense frontier: 0.189 at 495 PF (full fine-tune), 0.139 at 990 PF (LoRA), 0.101 at 1,963 PF (LoRA), 0.081 at 3,960 PF (full fine-tune), 0.078 at 3,986 PF (LoRA), 0.068 at 5,990 PF (LoRA), 0.064 at 7,934 PF (full fine-tune). FLOPs-to-match against it: LoRA 50% / 20% / 7% over three cuts 2.2x at 495 PF (0.136), 2.1x at 991 PF (0.100), 2.6x at 1,980 PF (0.072); LoRA 50% / 20% 2.0x, 2.3x, 2.0x; recipe 20% / 7% 1.8x, 2.0x, 2.1x (1,762 PF) and 1.9x (16x pool, 1,980 PF); full fine-tune 50% / 20% 1.6x at 991 PF and 1.9x at 1,970 PF; LoRA 10% / 3% 1.5x at 991 PF and 1.0x at 2,015 PF. So token dropping is worth about 2x in FLOPs (2.0-2.6x for the best arm) from 495 to 1,980 PF, with no decay as data grows; against dense full fine-tune alone 2.2-2.9x. At 3,975 PF on the 16x pool: LoRA 50% / 20% 0.064 (1.97x) and LoRA 50% / 20% / 7% 0.065 (1.88x), against dense LoRA 0.078 at 3,986 PF and dense full fine-tune 0.064 at 7,934 PF. The ratio stays near 2x over an 8-fold range of budgets (495 to 3,975 PF).

ideas.title: Early blocks forward-only under the drop
ideas.what: Blocks 0-6 run on every token and are now more than half of a drop arm's step cost. Freeze them (no adapters, no backward below the first cut), so the drop arms cost about 0.13-0.24x dense per step instead of 0.22-0.32x; the dense counterpart (dense LoRA with adapters from block 7) is run as the baseline, since freezing is available to dense training too. Budget-matched at 495 and 991 PF.
ideas.result: Negative (16k CE on 320 rows, one seed). At about 495 PF: dense LoRA with adapters only from block 7 0.205 (dense full fine-tune 0.189); frozen LoRA 50%/20%/7% 0.153 at 540 PF against 0.136 unfrozen at 493 PF; frozen LoRA 50%/20% 0.164 against 0.140; frozen recipe 0.174 against 0.146. At about 991 PF: frozen LoRA 50%/20%/7% 0.105 at 1,079 PF (1.7x) against 0.100 unfrozen at 989 PF (2.1x). The early blocks have to be trained. (My step counts assumed a cheaper frozen step than the meter measured, so the frozen arms ran 8-13% over budget; the ratios use the measured PF.)

ideas.title: Drop distractor documents at the input, on top of the token drop
ideas.what: The early blocks run on every token and are the cost floor. Remove a share of the non-gold documents of each row at the input (positions preserved, gold documents kept; uses the gold sidecar), constant or ramped up to the full row over training, and keep the 50% / 20% / 7% token drop above. Budget-matched at 495 PF, with dense LoRA + document subsampling as the control and per-task losses reported because removing distractors changes the outlier task.

best_by_hour.note: First 16k results; recomputed against the tuned reference (dense LoRA at LR 2e-5 is slightly better than at 1e-5). Worst-task speedup is at the 80-step level. One seed, eval_size 184.

best_by_hour.level: own final loss 0.159 (between the 50- and 60-step levels)
best_by_hour.note: Matched-loss ratio vs dense LoRA; 1.25x the recipe at that loss. Stopped by the 12-minute cap at step 143; a deeper two-seed confirmation is running. One seed, eval_size 184.
